items.question: A request reads: "Write a 3-bullet note for my manager, like: 'Sales: up 4%, ahead of plan.'" Which part is missing?

options.text: The context: the figures to write from
The task: what the note should do
options.why: "Write a note" is the task.

options.text: The format: the shape of the note
options.why: "3 bullets" is the format.

options.text: An example: one sample line
options.why: The sales bullet is an example.

feedback.correct: No context: it has nothing to write the note from.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the request for each of the four parts.

explain.text: It says what to write, in what shape, with a sample. But it gives no figures or report to write from. So the likely reply is invented figures in the right shape.

items.question: Which request is least likely to lead the chatbot to a fixed answer?

options.text: What are the main risks and benefits of this fund?
Why is this fund such a good choice?
options.why: It assumes the fund is good, so the likely reply argues that.

options.text: This fund is clearly too risky, agreed?
options.why: It asks for agreement, and agreement is the likely reply.

options.text: Prove that this fund will beat the market.
options.why: It assumes the conclusion and asks for support.

feedback.correct: Asking for risks and benefits leaves the answer open.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the request that assumes nothing.

explain.text: A leading request builds its answer into the question, and the likely reply goes along with it. Asking for both risks and benefits assumes nothing.

items.question: You ask a chatbot with no live data: "What will this share close at on Friday?" Which reply is best?

options.text: "No one can know Friday's close. I can explain what tends to move the price."
"It will close at £4.12, judging by its recent trading pattern."
options.why: No one can know a future close. A precise figure is invented.

options.text: "Probably between £4.10 and £4.15."
options.why: A narrow range is still a guess dressed as knowledge.

options.text: "It closed at £4.08 yesterday, so £4.08."
options.why: It cannot know yesterday's close either, and yesterday is not Friday.

feedback.correct: The honest reply says it cannot know, and offers what it can do.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether anyone could know the answer.

explain.text: A future price is unknowable, so any figure is invented. A good request invites the honest reply, and a good reply gives it.

items.question: A chatbot says 6% of £3,500 is £2,100. What does a quick estimate show?

options.text: It is ten times too big: 6% of £3,500 is about £210
It looks about right
options.why: 1% of £3,500 is £35, so 6% is £210. £2,100 is ten times that.

options.text: It is too small
options.why: It is too big, by ten times.

options.text: It is about double the right figure
options.why: It is ten times the right figure, not double.

feedback.correct: 6% of £3,500 is £210, so £2,100 has the decimal point in the wrong place.

explain.text: 1% of £3,500 is £35, so 6% is £210. The chatbot's £2,100 is ten times too big. An estimate catches a slip like this in seconds.

items.question: A chatbot says 12% of £2,350 is £305.50. Build 12% from 10% and 2%. What is it, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find 10% and 2%, then add.

byKey.bot: That is the chatbot's figure, which is 13% of £2,350. Build 12% yourself.
byKey.ten-only: That is 10% only. Add 2%, which is £47.
byKey.tenth: The decimal point slipped. 10% of £2,350 is £235.

explain.text: 10% of £2,350 is £235 and 2% is £47, so 12% is £282. The chatbot's £305.50 is 13%.

items.question: A chatbot says £5,000 at 4% a year, compounded, for 3 years grows to £5,600. What is the right balance, to the nearest penny?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.04 three times.

byKey.simple: That is simple interest, the chatbot's slip. Each year's 4% is on the grown balance.
byKey.two-years: You multiplied by 1.04 twice. Three years need three.

explain.text: Multiplying by 1.04 three times gives $5000 \times 1.04^3 = 5624.32$. The chatbot added 4% of £5,000 three times, which is simple interest.

items.question: A chatbot cites a real report for a figure. You open the report at the cited page and the figure is not there. What follows?

options.text: The figure is unsupported until you find it somewhere you can read
The figure is supported, because the report is real
options.why: A real report that does not say the figure supports nothing.

options.text: The figure must be on another page, so use it
options.why: Maybe, maybe not. Find it before you use it.

options.text: The report must be fake
options.why: You found it, so it is real. It just does not say this.

feedback.correct: Unsupported. A source counts only if it says the claim.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the three parts of a checked source.

explain.text: A source is checked when it is found, read at the cited part, and says the claim. The third part fails here, so the figure is unsupported.

items.question: A draft says "UK unemployment was 4.4% last quarter". The figure came from a chatbot. What is the best check?

options.text: The official statistics for that quarter, on the same measure
Ask the chatbot to confirm the figure for that quarter
options.why: Its confirmation is likely text.

options.text: A blog post that quotes a figure
options.why: A blog may copy a wrong figure or another quarter. Go to the publisher.

options.text: Your own memory of the news
options.why: Memory is a rough guide, not a check of a figure going to print.

feedback.correct: Go to the publisher of the official figure, for the right period and measure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where an official figure lives.

explain.text: An official figure is checked against the body that publishes it, for the right period and the right measure. Anything else may be a copy, or a guess.

lines: You: My salary is £1,200 a month. It rises 5%, then 5% again. What is it now? Show your working.
Step 2: after the first rise it is £1,260.
Step 4: after the second rise it is £1,320.
params.title: An invented example

items.question: A salary of £1,200 a month rises 5%, then rises 5% again. Tap the step that goes wrong.

feedback.correct: Step 3 takes 5% of £1,200 again; the second rise is on £1,260, so it is £63 and the salary ends at £1,323.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what each 5% is taken of.

byKey.l5: Step 4 follows from step 3; the slip is in step 3.

explain.text: The second rise is on the new salary, £1,260, so it is £63 and the salary ends at £1,323. Step 3 reused the old base. The working let you find exactly where.

items.question: You need the exact total of 500 invoices for the accounts. Which tool should do the sum?

options.text: A spreadsheet, with a rough estimate as a check
A chatbot, asked to show its working
options.why: 500 steps of working is too long to check, and the sum must be exact.

options.text: Two chatbots, comparing totals
options.why: Two sets of likely text that agree are still not an exact sum.

options.text: A rough estimate alone
options.why: An estimate gives the size, not the exact total.

feedback.correct: A spreadsheet adds exactly; an estimate checks the size.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which tool adds exactly.

explain.text: An exact total of many numbers is a job for a spreadsheet or a script. A rough estimate still checks that the result is the right size.
